expected_evidence: geological: a continent-spanning 'Younger Dryas Boundary' (YDB) sedimentary layer (~12,900 cal BP / ~10,950 BCE) containing elevated nanodiamonds (hexagonal lonsdaleite, cubic diamonds), magnetic spherules, iridium/platinum anomalies, and charcoal/soot layers indicative of impact-ejecta fallout and continental wildfires

material: microscopic impact-derived materials in stratified sediment cores/lake beds and archaeological (Clovis-era) site profiles across North America — melt glass, carbon spherules, shocked quartz grains

astronomical: a plausible source crater or airburst signature (e.g., over the Laurentide ice sheet or a Great Lakes/Hiawatha-type structure) — largely absent/unconfirmed in the real record, which is a major point of contention
genetic: megafauna population bottleneck or extinction signatures in ancient DNA dated to the YD onset, and possible human population genetic discontinuity in North America at this time

model_prior: the published Younger Dryas Impact Hypothesis literature (Firestone et al. 2007 and subsequent Comet Research Group papers) claiming YDB markers at 50+ sites, counterbalanced by strong critical/failed-replication literature (Pigati et al. 2012, Daulton et al. 2010/2017, van Hoesel et al. 2012, Holliday & Meltzer) disputing the nanodiamond/spherule identifications and the impact interpretation itself

iconographic/oral_tradition: essentially none expected — no writing systems existed in North America at this date, and any oral-tradition linkage (e.g., flood/fire myths) would be far too indirect and undateable to count as evidence
response.rationale: The interval (-10,950) corresponds to the Younger Dryas onset (~12,900 cal BP), so the 'younger-dryas' row is the appropriate detectability context rather than 'upper-paleolithic' broadly. In that row, geological (0.65) and astronomical (0.7) evidence types have relatively high detectability, since fine-grained sedimentary/lake-core stratigraphy from this period is routinely preserved and sampled by Quaternary geologists, and impact ejecta (spherules, nanodiamonds, iridium anomalies) are chemically/physically robust enough to persist for ~13,000 years in undisturbed sediment. Material evidence (0.35) is lower because organic/manufactured artifacts from Paleoindian contexts are sparse and taphonomically fragile, though this isn't the primary evidence class for an impact-ejecta hypothesis anyway. Genetic (0.3) and textual/oral_tradition/iconographic (~0-0.1) are appropriately low or negligible since no writing existed and ancient genomic material this old is hard to recover, especially when trying to link it directly to an impact event. Notably, this hypothesis maps closely onto the real, actively debated Younger Dryas Impact Hypothesis (Firestone et al. 2007 and successors): researchers have specifically searched for and reported (as well as failed to replicate) YDB nanodiamond/spherule/iridium layers at dozens of sites across North America and beyond. This means the evidence-search process has genuinely occurred with mixed, contested results — this is not simply an absence-of-evidence-due-to-low-detectability scenario, but one where moderate-to-good detectability enabled real (if disputed) empirical claims and rebuttals. I set the aggregate detectability adjustment to 0.55, reflecting that geological/astronomical channels are quite viable for this kind of event, material/genetic channels are moderate, and the overall proposition is empirically testable and has in fact been tested, even though current scientific consensus leans skeptical of the impact interpretation. Any recalled details about Firestone et al., Pigati, Daulton, or van Hoesel studies are drawn from model-prior (training-derived, unverified within this pipeline) rather than from evidence text provided directly to me in this session.
